passages.context: The Talmud's treatment of when a meal is legally over, read in the retrieved response for the whole folio. Registered as the decisive negative for the modern folded-napkin claim: the exact question the alleged custom would answer is answered here, in a household with servants, by the removal of the table.
passages.notes: The source's quotation marks around the reported speech are omitted from the transcription. The exchange continues with R. Zera's question and Raba's reply that they depend upon the Exilarch's tray.

passages.context: The Talmud's discussion of Mishnah Berakhot 8:3, read in the retrieved response for the whole folio. Registered as the evidence that the ancient rabbinic law of the table napkin is a ritual-purity question about where a damp hand-towel may be laid, with no servant, no folding, and no signal.
passages.notes: Two intervening exchanges of the discussion, on whether one vessel can defile another and whether a vessel can defile a man, stand between the two transcribed lines in the source and are omitted.

work.author: Rabbinic sages (Babylonian redaction)
work.description: The Babylonian Talmud's tractate on blessings. Folio 42a discusses when a meal is legally over and answers the question with the removal of the table; folio 52b discusses the Shammai and Hillel dispute about where a damp hand-towel may be laid at a meal. Loci use standard Vilna folio-and-side numbering.
work.title: Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Berakhot
